text: days post-transplant may be related to reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppressive therapy.22 It has a worse prognosis, with reports of up to half of patients de- veloping graft loss.21 Corticosteroids are used in the first- line treatment of acute rejection.11,23 For corticosteroid-re- sistant rejection, muromonab-CD3 or antilymphocyte im- munoglobulins are used, and increasing the dose of tac- rolimus, or conversion from ciclosporin to tacrolimus, may also be effective.2,4,9 Interleukin-2 receptor antibodies may also be used. Mycophenolate mofetil or sirolimus have been added to treat recurrent acute rejection.23 Chronic rejection is almost always preceded by one or more episodes of corticosteroid-resistant acute rejec- tion,21,22 and although its incidence has decreased5,21-23 to less than 5%, it remains difficult to treat. Corticosteroids are generally ineffective; conversion from ciclosporin to tacrolimus has been reported to be effective,21 as has addi- tion of mycophenolate mofetil to tacrolimus, followed by interleukin-2 receptor antibodies, and then sirolimus in non-responsive patients.23 The main complications encountered with liver trans- plants are infection in the early post-transplant period, vas- cular and biliary complications, recurrent disease (particu- larly viral recurrence), and adverse effects due to immunosuppressants.4,6,22,23 Sepsis is an important cause of death in the early post- transplant period.6,24,25 Patients at increased risk, including those with malnutrition, fulminant liver failure, or renal in- sufficiency, require particularly cautious immunosuppres- sion and more aggressive antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis regimens. Recurrence of hepatitis B infection is common.26 Al- though the introduction of hepatitis B immunoglobulins and lamivudine have improved the prospects for these pa- tients, combination antiviral therapy and a modified im- munosuppression protocol are usually needed.3,6,7,20,21 Hepatitis C recurrence is almost universal in infected pa- tients,11,21,27 with a probable reduction in long-term graft survival.7,20,21 The use of corticosteroids and muromonab- CD3 appears to be associated with more severe recurrence of hepatitis C.
